name: Paul Skenes
season_outlook: Just 23 years old, Skenes is already authoring one heck of a career story. The No. 1 pick in the 2023 Draft, Skenes breezed to the majors after only 12 minor league starts and struck out 11 batters over six no-hit innings in his second career game on his way to winning the 2024 NL Rookie of the Year Award. He also became the first player in history to start the All-Star Game in both of his first two seasons, won the 2025 NL Cy Young Award and posted the lowest ERA (1.99) of any pitcher through his first 46 career starts. If there's a nit to pick, it's that his Pirates provided him such little run support (3.38 runs, third worst among ERA qualifiers) that he won only 10 games despite leading the majors in ERA in 2025. But hey, they're at least a little better offensively entering 2026? Skenes is as good a bet as any to lead all pitchers in fantasy points as well as the Player Rater.

name: Shohei Ohtani
season_outlook: Baseball's greatest historical two-way player could be primed for his best season yet. On offense in 2025, Ohtani exceeded 50 home runs for a second consecutive season and stole 20-plus bases for a third straight year. On the mound, the Dodgers were uber-conservative with his recovery from his September 2023 elbow reconstruction, but Ohtani delivered per-start numbers in line with his pre-injury rates. His pitching usage also ramped up right in time for the playoffs, during which he became the first player in history to hit three home runs while also striking out 10 batters in one game in the Dodgers' NLCS clincher, triggering memories of his 2022, when he scored 411 fantasy points as a hitter and 475 as a pitcher. As the Dodgers surely will, so must you manage his daily utility -- he can be used as a DH or pitcher, but not both --  but Ohtani's potential puts him head and shoulders ahead of the pack.

name: Yoshinobu Yamamoto
season_outlook: After a rocky first year in the U.S., year number two for Yamamoto was consistently excellent from start to finish -- literally. He won both the season's first game (in Japan in March) and its last, Game 7 of the World Series. In sum, he posted top-6 numbers across the league in ERA, WHIP and strikeout rate. Yamamoto's innings spike, totaling 211 frames between the regular season and postseason after 112 2/3 the year before, represents a slight concern following the rotator cuff issues he experienced in 2023, but his Dodgers are as careful with managing pitchers as any team in baseball. He's a fantasy ace and should be drafted in the opening rounds as such.

name: Max Fried
season_outlook: Fried settled in nicely in his first year in pinstripes, setting personal bests in wins (19), starts (32), innings pitched (195 1/3) and strikeouts (189). He performed consistently excellent outside of an eight-start, July/early August stretch in which his control wavered (6.80 ERA, 8.3 BB%). These days, that's the description of a fantasy ace, as few pitchers are spared the occasional wart, and most have similar, minor injury questions to what's in Fried's past. He's one of the higher-floor options at the position, and one of the few pitchers who, health willing, seems likely to exceed the 200-IP threshold. Build your staff around him with confidence.

name: Chris Sale
season_outlook: Through 15 starts, Sale was on track to defend his 2024 Cy Young, carrying a 2.52 ERA and 1.16 WHIP with 114 strikeouts across 89.1 innings before a fractured left ribcage sidelined him for a little more than 10 weeks. He returned without missing a beat, logging a 2.72 ERA and 0.83 WHIP over his final six starts and striking out 51 in 36.1 frames. On the season, the underlying skills remained elite, as his 26.1 strikeout-minus-walk percentage ranked fourth among pitchers with at least 120 innings. While the injury underscores the health risk attached to the left-hander entering his age-37 season, the fact that it was not arm-related has kept early drafters confident, with Sale still among the first 10 starters selected.

name: Cristopher Sanchez
season_outlook: Much of the storyline surrounding Sanchez during last year's breakthrough was his second straight year of increased sinker velocity -- he went from 92.1 mph in 2023 to 94.5 in 2024 to 95.4 in 2025 -- but the real story was the advances he made with his changeup. He struck out 130 batters with that pitch alone, the most by any pitcher in six years. Sanchez dodged a minor scare with his elbow in April, swiftly rebounding to post more quality starts than any pitcher, as well as the third-best ERA from that point forward. His combination of pinpoint control, extreme ground ball repertoire and top-shelf stuff make him one of the safest investments on the pitching side (if there is such a thing in this modern age). Draft Sanchez as your fantasy ace with confidence.

name: Mason Miller
season_outlook: For a pitcher to possess as stuff as filthy as Miller's is flat-out unfair. Among those who have thrown at least 400 of either pitch in any of the 18 seasons for which we have pitch data, Miller's 101.2-mph average fastball velocity last season was second highest, while his 54.6% whiff rate with his slider was 15th. Though his deadline deal to the Padres bumped him from his prior closer role, he thrived in setup relief with his new team, scoring the sixth-most fantasy points (124) despite not winning a game and posting only two saves in that time. Robert Suarez's winter departure paved the way for Miller to reclaim the ninth-inning role in San Diego, from which the right-hander has a wide-open path to being the top performing relief pitcher in fantasy baseball in 2026.

name: Dylan Cease
season_outlook: If you believe in such folly, it's an even-numbered year, so based upon past patterns, Cease is destined for greatness in 2026. He's a modern-day Bret Saberhagen, but with strikeouts! Cease's FIP tells a more rational tale, as he has fluctuated by less than two-thirds of a run in the category over the past five seasons, a signal that luck factors have been friendly to him in those even-numbered campaigns, but harsh in odd years. What fuels bounce-back chatter with Cease isn't the date on the calendar, but rather his new team's defense, as the Blue Jays are significantly better in the field than were the 2025 Padres. See, luck can be controlled � somewhat, at least. Don't let Cease slip beyond the first few rounds of your draft.

name: Tarik Skubal
season_outlook: Don't let the persistent trade rumors swirling around him dissuade you that Skubal is as good a choice to lead your fantasy pitching staff as anyone. He's coming off back-to-back Cy Youngs, and has made consistent, notable improvements in almost every statistical category across his six MLB seasons. Skubal set personal bests in ERA, WHIP, walk rate, K/BB rate, whiff rate and rate of hard contact allowed in 2025. Since July 1, 2023, he has a 2.37 ERA and MLB-leading totals in both wins (38) and strikeouts (571). He's also entering his contract year -- the very reason for said trade rumors -- which, while hardly a guarantee as a motivating factor, assures he'll play 2026 at full bore, and with a team that will provide him the necessary support to again thrive.

name: Jacob deGrom
season_outlook: Fully recovered from June 2023 Tommy John surgery, deGrom in 2025 made more starts (30) and pitched more innings (172 2/3) than he had in any season since his back-to-back Cy Young seasons of 2018-19, remarkably doing so at the age of 37. He exhibited similarly elite average fastball velocity (97.5 mph) and whiff rate on his slider (39.0%), yet couldn't match the lofty strikeout rates, to those prime years. That's not unexpected from a pitcher at deGrom's age, and injury setbacks will remain a worry for the remainder of his career. An extreme fly-ball lean over his final 10 starts (an MLB-leading 42.1%) also heightens regression concerns. He still has what it takes to be a fantasy ace, but the steep downside present in his profile also makes him a dicey leading-man pick.

name: George Kirby
season_outlook: One of the best control specialists in baseball, Kirby's 2025 was sidetracked by shoulder inflammation that cost him most of spring training and nearly two regular-season months. He'd rebound with 11 quality starts, a 3.59 ERA and 4.95 K/BB ratio over his final 17 starts -- and he was productive in three of his four postseason starts. All of this offers encouragement for a 2026 rebound. Kirby's 3.6% walk rate over his first four MLB seasons is the second lowest by any pitcher in the modern era, and he has an underrated slider that's capable of generating strikeouts. There's risk here, but the prospective reward would easily place him among his position's top 10 performers.

name: Bryan Woo
season_outlook: Gifted with a high-90s fastball, blossoming sweeper and some of the most pinpoint control of anyone in baseball, Woo broke through in a big way in 2025. He finished fifth among pitchers in fantasy points, third in WHIP and K/BB ratio, fourth in quality starts (21) and fifth in wins. Perhaps most importantly, he remained healthy for long enough to make a career-high 30 starts. A pectoral strain in September limited his contributions during the team's playoff run, but the winter's rest should afford him the chance to heal and merely warrants a quick glance once spring training opens. Woo is a legitimate fantasy ace.

name: Cam Schlittler
season_outlook: Schlittler went from being a prospect afterthought entering the 2024 minor-league season to becoming the first pitcher in postseason history to pitch eight scoreless innings of at least 12 strikeouts (with zero walks) in the 2025 Wild Card Series. Such demonstrates the magnitude of his unexpected breakthrough. Thanks to his improved, 98.0-mph fastball and cutter, he scored the 19th-most fantasy points from the date of his July 9 debut forward, with stellar underlying metrics that support his ability to approach or match the effort over a full 2026. Schlittler is a strong mid-round, middle-of-your-staff pick for fantasy purposes, assuming the back issues that popped up as spring training dawned don't become a lingering issue.

name: Garrett Crochet
season_outlook: In two seasons since shifting from relief to the rotation, Crochet has handled the move with aplomb. His 2025 reflected significant gains, not only in the 59 1/3 additional innings he tallied, but also the near-run he shaved off his ERA as well as his doubling his number of quality starts (22) relative to 2024. Crochet also gained velocity over the course of the summer, a signal that he has now settled into his role as a staff ace. He was a model of consistency, the only pitcher to score as many as 73 fantasy points in each of the season's six months. He's an ideal pitcher around whom to build your team, and a first-round pick in points leagues.

name: Jacob Misiorowski
season_outlook: Misiorowski, one of the game's top prospects, arrived in the majors last June to pitch five no-hit innings in his first career start, and post a 2.81 ERA and 33.7% strikeout rate across his first five. Unfortunately, between his mediocre control and the shin contusion that cost him a 17-day stay on the IL, he couldn't maintain that pace the rest of the way and his ERA ballooned to 5.36 across his final nine starts and one relief appearance. Misiorowski's raw stuff, however, was consistently excellent, and if the Brewers trust him to pitch deeper into games, he could break out in a big way in 2026. There's danger here of overrating him, but among mid-round picks, he carries a lot of upside.

name: Logan Gilbert
season_outlook: A first-half flexor strain limited Gilbert to just 25 starts spanning 131 innings, breaking his streak of three straight seasons with at least 185 frames. The injury interrupted his best season ever, at least in terms of his ERA estimators. His actual ERA ran a little higher than expected despite Gilbert setting a new personal best with a 32.3 percent strikeout rate. Gilbert's 26.5 K-BB percentage was the third highest among all pitchers logging at least 130 innings. That jump came after he shelved his cutter in favor of more four-seamers, splitters and sliders, though the adjusted mix led to a modest uptick in walks. Even so, Gilbert enters the season as a key piece of one of the league's top rotations, pitching roughly half his games in the most favorable park for pitchers.

name: Freddy Peralta
season_outlook: After months of rumors, Peralta was traded from the Brewers to the Mets in January as he enters his final season before free agency. The right-hander put together a career year in 2025, leading the National League in wins with 17 to go along with a career-low 2.70 ERA across 33 starts for Milwaukee. Peralta has now reached the vaunted 30-start and 200-strikeout thresholds each of the last three years, cementing his status as a legitimate frontline starter in MLB, with three excellent secondary pitches making up for a mediocre fastball. It's entirely possible that 2025 will end up being the zenith of his career, as everything went right for him during the regular season. Regression should be built into the draft price, but the skills and track record at 29 years old make Peralta worthy of a significant investment.

name: Zack Wheeler
season_outlook: Wheeler was amid one of the most remarkable five-year runs of any active pitcher at the time he succumbed to thoracic outlet surgery last September. Even missing the season's final six weeks, from 2021-25, he ranked first among pitchers in fantasy points (2,327), first in WHIP (1.00), tied for first in quality starts (99), second in strikeouts (1,041), third in ERA (2.90), tied for third in wins (65), fourth in innings pitched (908) and fifth in K/BB ratio (5.10). Wheeler's recovery timetable should place a return sometime around May 1, though there are risks involved with the speed and effectiveness of pitchers' rehabilitation, and his advancing age (35) raises an additional concern. He showed no ill effects of the aging process before the operation, however, so if you're willing to stash him in an IL spot hoping he makes a swift recovery, he still has an ace's fantasy ceiling.

name: Cade Smith
season_outlook: After a massive rookie breakthrough in middle relief in 2024, Smith graduated to closer status last August, going 13-for-16 converting his saves with a 2.60 ERA and 39 K's compared to two walks over the season's final two months. Considering he was fantasy baseball's top point scorer among relievers during that time (162 points), there's every reason to believe he can contend for that status working in the role full-time in 2026. Smith has been especially dominant against left-handed hitters (.162/.218/.270 rates in his two MLB seasons), and he made big strides in minimizing hard contact last year -- a combination that makes him one of the safest investments at his position despite his limited closer experience.

name: Kevin Gausman
season_outlook: Two-pitch guys are supposed to be relievers and not starters, but Gausman never got that message as he continues to ride his heavy fastball-splitter approach to continued success as a major-league starter. Gausman's 2025 saw him work a career high in regular-season innings along with another 30 stressful postseason innings which might be a cause for concern heading into 2026 (see Zac Gallen from 2023 to 2024). Over the past five seasons, Gausman is one of just three pitchers with at least 1000 strikeouts and is tied for second in games started while also being second in innings pitched. Everything looks good for his skills, but workhorses eventually stop being workhorses, so proceed with a degree of caution.

name: Joe Ryan
season_outlook: Amidst a teardown in Minnesota, Ryan stood tall with a career-best 3.42 ERA over a career-high 171 innings in 2025. The right-hander was one of two Twins All-Stars, along with Byron Buxton. Ryan has emerged as one of the team's top starters over the last few seasons, though he could be on his way out in due time as the organization continues to rebuild. Ryan would be befitting of the ace label almost anywhere given that he ranks seventh among qualified starters in strikeout-minus-walk percentage over the last three seasons. Home runs and occasional injuries have held him back from reaching true greatness, but Ryan is only 29 and his best years may still be ahead of him. With six pitches and pinpoint control, Ryan can be drafted with confidence as an SP2 for fantasy leagues.

name: Chase Burns
season_outlook: The No. 2 overall pick in the 2024 Draft, Burns soared to the majors after only 13 minor-league starts, then used his 98.7-mph fastball and filthy slider to post four games of double-digit strikeouts in his first eight, as well as a 37.7% K rate over that time. While he had some issues with lefties and missed time due to a flexor strain, he did return to make five solid relief appearances and figures to make the Reds' rotation out of spring training. Burns has some work to do on improving a pitch to use against lefties, and he's a little too fly ball-oriented to avoid issues with homers in Great American Ball Park, but he's one of the most intriguing breakthrough candidates among pitchers. He's a dynasty league building block and a mid-round target in redraft formats.

name: Tyler Glasnow
season_outlook: Glasnow was unable to repeat his overall performance from 2024 when he set a new career high with just 134 innings of work, but did at least post a career-best 3.19 ERA over the 18 starts he made. The ERA was surprising since his walk rate jumped from 6.7 percent to 11.7 percent last season, dropping his normally stellar K-BB to a career-low 17.2 percent. Glasnow was still impossible to hit as the league hit .175 against him last season, which is not surprising since only Freddy Peralta, Jacob deGrom and Max Scherzer have been tougher to hit amongst all starting pitchers in baseball since Glasnow joined the league in 2016. Glasnow has some of the nastiest stuff in baseball, but he also has one of the most fragile bodies as something always breaks down. Expect 120 innings of valuable contributions but not much more.

name: Shota Imanaga
season_outlook: Imanaga is back with the Cubs for 2026 despite the team declining his three-year club option, since the club still tagged him with the qualifying offer, which ultimately led to the pitcher accepting it to re-prove his market viability next offseason. Imanaga had a hamstring injury in early May which kept him off the mound for six weeks. He made 20 starts before September and recorded eight wins with a 3.08 ERA, and 0.93 WHIP. However, his final five starts in September included a 6.51 ERA with velocity decline and 10 homers allowed in just 27.1 innings of work. Despite the decent overall numbers, his strikeout numbers dropped significantly to 7.3 K/9. The motivation is there for a great 2026, but are the skills?

name: Hunter Brown
season_outlook: After finishing seventh among pitchers in fantasy points over the final four months of 2024, Brown followed things up with six straight months of near-identical production (he'd finish sixth this time). A modest boost to his swinging-strike rate, while maintaining his elevated average fastball velocity, fueled a consistently excellent year, during which he never went more than three outings between quality starts. Brown appears to have leveled off, but he has done so as one of the premier talents at his position. He should be one of the first starting pitchers off your draft board in any format.

name: Gavin Williams
season_outlook: Williams took a sizable, statistical step forward in 2025, shaving more than a run and three-quarters off his ERA while reaching the 30-start plateau for the first time as a professional, but his skill set remained a bit of a mixed bag. He had the majors' worst qualified walk rate (11.8%), the widest negative ERA-FIP differential (-1.33) and poor metrics in terms of contact quality allowed, signaling regression coming due. Still, Williams is only 26 years old, equipped with a 96.6-mph fastball and a pair of elite breaking pitches (curveball, sweeper) that make him especially tough against lefties, giving him growth potential that could neutralize those luck factors. It's probably best to treat his draft stock similarly to his 2025 fantasy finishes: SP24 (points), SP28 (rotisserie).

name: Aroldis Chapman
season_outlook: The fireballer put together his best season ever at age 37, successfully converting 32 of 34 save chances for the Red Sox during the regular season with a career-low 1.17 ERA. Chapman was virtually untouchable in the ninth inning with his trademark fastball and nasty breaking pitch. Shockingly, he cut his walk rate down to a career-low mark of 6.6 percent after being at or above 15 percent each of the prior four seasons. It was the dramatic reversal in that particular department that fueled his renaissance, though it's understandable to be skeptical given his history of control woes. Signed to an extension last August, Chapman will return to the closer role to which he is highly accustomed and attempt to continue bucking historical trends with his dominance at an advanced age.

name: Jhoan Duran
season_outlook: A dominating ninth-inning force in Minnesota for 3.5 seasons, Duran's career truly took off following his deadline deal to the Phillies last July. Finally bestowed with a ninth-inning role all his own, the right-hander saved an MLB-leading 16 games for his new team, all the while maintaining his top-shelf, closer-caliber raw stuff. Duran returns in the same role for a competitive 2026 Phillies team, giving him a legitimate chance to contend for the fantasy points/Player Rater lead at his position. His combination of a 100-plus-mph fastball and whiff-generating knuckle curve make him one of the most attractive relief pitchers in drafts.

name: Logan Webb
season_outlook: Webb has logged the most innings of any pitcher over the past five seasons, throwing 40 more innings than any other pitcher. Over those 968.1 innings, he has logged a 3.19 ERA, 1.16 WHIP and an 18 K-BB percentage. He took his production up a level in 2025 striking out 224 batters, besting his previous career high by 30, and he did so in fewer innings than he he needed to set that previous personal record. Webb was once primarily a sinker-slider-changeup pitcher, but has also recently introduced a cutter and four-seamer to his repertoire and now both lefties and righties have to discern between five different offerings.  He is one of five pitchers to win at least 10 games in each of the past five seasons and there is little reason to think he will fall short of hitting his usual benchmarks in 2026.

name: Jesus Luzardo
season_outlook: In his seventh season in the majors, Luzardo finally parlayed his high-90s fastball and whiff-generating sweeper and changeup into the breakthrough year fantasy managers had long anticipated. In fact, if not for back-to-back starts early in the season in which he surrendered a combined 20 earned runs, he might have garnered Cy Young votes and been a more prominent name heading into 2026 drafts. No matter, as that might make Luzardo a potential fantasy ace at the price of a mid-staff starter. He's no longer quite the injury risk he once was, with a pair of 32-start seasons in the past three years and, while he calls one of the more hitter-friendly environments his home, he gets some of the best lineup and bullpen support of any pitcher in the league.

name: David Bednar
season_outlook: Bednar's overall 2025 numbers were so good that you almost forget he was sent to Triple-A early in the season because he got off to such an awful start. Bednar had a rough spring and then blew two of his first three save chances opening weekend with some bad command and worse batted-ball luck which led Pittsburgh to send him to Indianapolis for some fine-tuning. Bednar returned three weeks later and was utterly dominant as a closer, winning six games and saving 26 more while striking out 83 batters and limited opposing hitters to a .183 average in his time between the Pirates and Yankees. Whereas he was a fringe top closer option heading into 2025, he is now a firm first-closer option in 2026 with the Yankees fully confident in Bednar's abilities as evidenced by them letting Devin Williams and Luke Weaver depart in free agency.

name: Michael King
season_outlook: Injuries derailed King's 2025, from the shoulder inflammation that cost him nine weeks around midseason, to the left knee inflammation that cost him one month just one start into his return from the former ailment. His raw stuff suffered accordingly (and predictably), though the winter's rest and a strong Cactus League showing could restore his potential as one of the position's top 20. When at his best, King has four offerings that generate at least a 25% whiff rate (four-seamer, changeup, sweeper and slider), and he's one of the better pitchers at suppressing hard contact. Let his March drive your draft decision, but he's at least a worthwhile risk/reward middle rounder.

name: Andres Munoz
season_outlook: After two seasons of his elite velocity and swing-and-miss skills toiling in a closer's timeshare in manager Scott Servais' matchups-oriented bullpen, Munoz thrived as the Mariners' full-time guy in Dan Wilson's first full season calling the shots. Munoz finished second in fantasy points among relief pitchers, third in saves and fourth in ERA, not to mention he added 8 1/3 shutout innings and two saves in the Mariners' two-round playoff run. He'll return in the same role, for a similarly competitive team, meaning another run as a top-five fantasy closer seems likely.

name: Blake Snell
season_outlook: For what seemed like the umpteenth year in a row, Snell was excellent when available to his fantasy managers � which didn't happen especially often. Among the 61 pitchers who have made at least 87 starts over the last four seasons, he ranks first in strikeout rate (31.9%), second in ERA (2.76), fifth in fantasy points per start (13.9) and seventh in hard-hit rate allowed (34.8%). The problem? That's exactly the number of starts Snell made in that time, which is under 22 per year. It's remarkable that he has been able to maintain such a high level of productivity around his many absences, but credit the Dodgers for being among the best at maximizing pitcher workloads and utility when available. We see no reason for that to change now. So, how lucky do you feel?

name: Bryce Elder
season_outlook: Elder's 5.30 ERA and 1.39 WHIP over 28 starts in 2025 are ugly on the surface, though his 2.82 ERA and 0.99 WHIP across his final seven starts provide some reason for optimism heading into 2026.  He cut down on the walks (2.9 BB/9) but also struck out fewer batters (7.5 K/9) compared to 2024. Atlanta will be looking to return to contention after a down year, and the right-hander may need to carry that late-season form into spring training in order to have a chance of making the Opening Day rotation. Regardless, Elder is likely to make some starts for Atlanta at some point in 2026, but his days could be numbered if he struggles early on.

name: Spencer Strider
season_outlook: Strider's recovery from an April 2024 UCL repair -- his second such major elbow surgery -- got off to a solid start, as he had two games with double-digit strikeouts and averaged 12.3 fantasy points across his first 12 starts. Diminished fastball velocity and a ballooning walk rate would undermine him thereafter, as he had a 5.46 ERA and averaged just 4.3 fantasy points over his final 11 turns. It's difficult to pinpoint the reasons behind Strider's late struggles, with the easiest explanation being the challenging road back from UCL surgery, but his inconsistency is a concern for fantasy managers. When healthy, he has elite stuff that can make him one of the best pitchers in the game, but the risk involved makes him more of a middle-of-your-staff type come 2026 drafts.

name: Framber Valdez
season_outlook: A model of consistency, durability and elevated floors among pitchers, Valdez hit a rough patch over 2025's final two months, which could explain why he lingered on the free agent market for so long. A .330 BABIP and 60.8 LOB% hinted that his 6.05 ERA during that time was more mirage than trend, while the left-hander's 83 quality starts, 767 2/3 innings pitched and 1,659 fantasy points from 2022-25 combined (all of which ranked top-three at his position) provide fairer perspective on his skills. As an extreme ground baller, Valdez's only team-influenced effect would be the infield defense behind him. The Tigers’ group is strong enough to assure him another potential top-15 fantasy starter stat line.

name: Raisel Iglesias
season_outlook: Iglesias finished one save shy of his third straight 30-save season, largely due to early-season struggles that led to a temporary demotion from the closer role in early June. He carried a 6.75 ERA and 1.54 WHIP on June 5 after blowing his fourth save. Following five scoreless outings spanning four innings, with two holds and a win, Iglesias reclaimed primary closing duties. He then posted a 1.37 ERA and 0.69 WHIP the rest of the way, converting 21 of 22 save chances. While ERA swings are often variance-driven, Iglesias leaned more heavily on his four-seamer in the second half while nearly shelving his slider, which helped address the home-run issues from earlier in the season. Atlanta signed the veteran to a one-year, $16 million deal, ostensibly to close, but the team also added last year's saves leader, Robert Suarez.

name: Riley O'Brien
season_outlook: A 31-year-old journeyman, O'Brien added velocity to his sinker and spin to his slider and broke through for the 2025 Cardinals, ultimately earning himself their closer job in the month of September. That might give him a leg up in their spring competition for the role, and his ground ball leaning and ability to suppress hard contact does minimize the downside if he emerges. Monitor O'Brien's spring progress, which will ultimately decide whether holds or saves are his target, but there's enough opportunity here to make him a viable fantasy late-rounder.

name: Nathan Eovaldi
season_outlook: Eovaldi threw a shutout in his second start of 2025 and pitched like a Cy Young candidate with a 1.73 ERA and 0.85 WHIP over 22 total starts for the Rangers before a rotator cuff strain ended his season in late August. The right-hander then underwent sports hernia surgery in October. While ostensibly healthy heading into 2026, Eovaldi should be considered a long shot to make 30 starts, something he's done only once over the last decade. Regression to his numbers seems inevitable, though tangible improvement can be found behind his success last season, as he dialed back his fastball usage in strategic fashion while trimming his walk rate back to elite territory. As he enters his age-36 season, the wheels are in danger of falling off, but Eovaldi is a legitimate ace when healthy.

name: Gerrit Cole
season_outlook: Baseball's top-scoring fantasy pitcher over the first four seasons of his Yankees career (2020-23), Cole missed the first three months of 2024 due to an elbow injury, then ultimately succumbed to 2025-ending Tommy John surgery last March. A 14-month recovery timetable would have him ready to rejoin the big-league club in May, though the variability of return date and initial performance level coming off that operation lends uncertainty to his 2026 draft stock. Cole will be one of the most important pitchers to track once he resumes game competition (exhibition or minor-league level) in the spring, but his skill set makes him one of the best IL stashes for prospective front-of-a-staff fantasy production in the season's second half (or even its final four months).

name: Cole Ragans
season_outlook: A rotator cuff strain cost Ragans three months of 2025, entirely thwarting his rise to becoming one of fantasy baseball's premier starters. That, coupled with a groin strain that cost him 19 days in May/June, cast him as somewhat of an injury risk entering 2026, but be aware that these ailments did little to diminish his excellent skill set. Ragans' final two regular-season starts (among the three he made in September) had him striking out 18 out of 35 batters, with similar levels of velocity and swing-and-miss rates to those pre-injury. He'll need careful examination during spring training for any lingering health issues, but a dominant Ragans in March could help make a case for him to be a top-10 fantasy starter come draft day.

name: Sonny Gray
season_outlook: Gray and Lady Luck have been at odds for the last two years. In 2024, his ERA was pegged about a run too high by xFIP, and last season, his 4.28 ERA was deemed roughly a run higher than its estimators. His BABIP and HR/FB rate were elevated, while his LOB percentage was suppressed. Gray eclipsed 180 frames for the second straight season, which he had last accomplished in 2015. For the second consecutive season, his velocity slipped, but he waived his no-trade clause to join the Red Sox, who specialize in teaching pitchers to work off breaking balls and offspeed stuff, and Gray can throw multiple types. Gray's home runs have crept up over the past two seasons, and the Green Monster has a habit of turning routine flyballs into doubles, so Gray may need to get back in favor with Lady Luck. Father Time looms, but for now, Gray remains dependable.

name: Devin Williams
season_outlook: One of 2025's biggest disappointments, Williams simply couldn't get the job done in the ninth for the Yankees. It took him just one month to get removed as their closer, after he surrendered as many earned runs in that time (10) as he had during the entirety of his career-year 2023. His season-ending ERA wound up being nearly three full runs higher than the total over his first six MLB seasons. In Williams' strong defense, however, he had outrageous numbers over the final four months in terms of batting average allowed (.172) and strikeout rate (38.6%) -- and he was done in by a 55.2 LOB% that was lower than any qualified reliever had posted in three years. The Mets, who signed him to serve as their 2026 closer, surely saw this and expect a full rebound. We tend to agree.

name: Brandon Woodruff
season_outlook: Despite Woodruff recently missing the better part of two years and ending 2025 back on the injured list with a lat strain, Milwaukee extended him the qualifying offer for 2026, which speaks to just how well he pitched when available last season. After his recovery from 2023 shoulder surgery was set back several times, Woodruff finally returned with five quality starts in his first six outings before enduring a couple hiccups in August. His xBA and xERA were both among the very best in baseball in his limited sample of 64.2 big-league innings last season. The right-hander has always gotten whiffs and the Brewers have proven they know what they're doing in regards to pitching. Chasing a full season's worth of starts would be a fool's errand, but the team clearly has high hopes for Woodruff in regards to both performance and workload.

name: Edwin Diaz
season_outlook: From a rates perspective, Diaz's 2025 was up there alongside any of his best statistical seasons, including his outrageous, 57-save 2018. The main drawback was his garnering only 31 save chances -- an inexplicably low total for a closer from an 83-win team. Diaz departed the Mets during the winter for a Dodgers team that has finished second in the majors in save chances in both of the last two seasons, despite their never truly having a singular ninth-inning choice over that time. While manager Dave Roberts could exploit a matchup every now and then, Diaz's contract and raw stuff almost assuredly will earn him the role for 2026, from which the right-hander is as good a bet to top his position in fantasy value as anyone.

name: Eury Perez
season_outlook: Perez's return from April 2024 Tommy John surgery offered far more promise in terms of his underlying metrics than what his surface numbers indicated. Among pitchers with at least as many as his 20 starts, he ranked second in average fastball velocity (97.9 mph), fifth in BAA (.195) and 15th in strikeout rate (27.3%). Perez also finished the year with a flourish, averaging 16.0 fantasy points over his final four starts, further underscoring his growth potential heading into 2026. Expect the Marlins to be cautious with their 22-year-old, soon-to-be-ace, but he's one of the best upside picks among starting pitchers.

name: Ranger Suarez
season_outlook: Although a back issue cost him the first month-plus of 2025, Suarez swiftly recaptured his prior form as one of the game's best command artists, as for the fifth consecutive season he placed in at least the 70th percentile in terms of average exit velocity and hard-hit rate allowed. In fact, he tied for the season's longest consecutive quality start streak (10, May 10-June 29). These things appealed to the Red Sox, who, despite an overstuffed rotation, brought him on as a reliable, middle-of-the-staff innings eater. Fantasy managers should regard him the same way, understanding that such pitchers typically carry a little more value in points than rotisserie leagues.

name: Taj Bradley
season_outlook: Bradley had an underwhelming 4.61 ERA in 21 starts for Tampa Bay in 2025 before being traded to Minnesota, where he struggled even more with a 6.61 ERA in six outings. He posted a career-worst 8.0 K/9 and 3.5 BB/9 last season but also had a career-best 1.2 HR/9. Bradley has shown flashes of brilliance since making his MLB debut in 2023 but has been mostly ineffective, with the drop in strikeouts negating the one area in which he still provided fantasy value. Bradley isn't guaranteed to begin 2026 with a spot in Minnesota's rotation, but the Twins seem likely to give him a chance to get back on track in the big leagues given how hard they committed to selling at the trade deadline last summer.

name: Nick Pivetta
season_outlook: After eight mediocre seasons between Philadelphia and Boston, Pivetta broke out in his first year with San Diego in 2025, going 13-5 with a 2.87 ERA and 0.99 WHIP across a career-high 181.2 innings during the regular season. Not only had Pivetta never posted an ERA under 3.00 prior to last year, he hadn't posted a mark under 4.00. A flyball pitcher, Pivetta has often struggled with homers, but he cut his home-run rate way down and was especially stingy with the long ball at home in Petco Park. Although he hadn't enjoyed a high level of success prior to 2025, Pivetta often tantalized with his strikeout rates. The late bloomer will continue to take the ball every fifth day for the Padres, and expectations should be heightened but realistic.

name: Josh Hader
season_outlook: No other active closer has more saves than Hader over the past five seasons. His 28.8 strikeout-minus-walk percentage lead all closers in that time, as well. Throw in the fourth-best WHIP and the second-best batting average against, and you may ask yourself why there is any reason Hader is not the first closer off the board in fantasy drafts. The answer to that question lies in the uncertainty surrounding his health, as he came down with shoulder soreness in early August and never returned to the mound, then dealt with biceps inflammation at the onset of spring training. It is also worth remembering that Hader was coming off a post-COVID high for workload from 2024 to 2025, which could help explain the injuries. Keep tabs on his progress as Opening Day approaches.

name: Michael Wacha
season_outlook: Wacha is coming off a season in which he threw the most innings he has worked since his 181.1 frames way back in 2015. Wacha has avoided the injured list the past two seasons and continues to provide consistent if boring production to fantasy managers with safe ratios and a below-average strikeout rate. Wacha has a deep repertoire of pitches built around his changeup, and he will throw all six pitches to both righties and lefties, using his abilities to keep hitters off balance to make up for what he lacks in velocity. This approach is a perfect fit for pitching in Kansas City where Wacha has allowed just 13 home runs since joining the club compared to 19 in his road starts. This season should be yet another consistently steady campaign for the veteran, but you will need to find your strikeouts from other pitchers.

name: Clay Holmes
season_outlook: After a three-year run as the Yankees' closer and seven years in MLB as a reliever, Holmes signed with the Mets as a starter in December of 2024 and held his own last season in his first year as a full-time starter. The right-hander had his workload managed down the stretch but finished 2025 with a 3.53 ERA, 1.30 WHIP and 129:66 K:BB across 165.2 innings (33 appearances). His move to the rotation predictably resulted in reduction in velocity and strikeouts, but Holmes was able to mostly offset that by being one of the most prolific groundball starters in baseball (55.9 percent groundball rate). A 7.0 K/9 certainly lowers Holmes' upside, but he'll still have a fair amount of fantasy value if he can replicate his run prevention from 2025.

name: Nick Lodolo
season_outlook: Lodolo made huge strides in 2025, posting a 4.8% walk rate that ranked sixth among pitchers with at least 20 starts, while generating many swings-and-misses on pitches out of the zone -- he had the fourth-best chase rate among that same group -- before injuries largely interrupted his final two months. At the time, he had scored the 20th-most fantasy points among pitchers. Whether those injuries (a blister, an illness, a right groin issue) represent a recurring pattern is in question, but Lodolo could be on the verge of a full-season breakthrough with the adjustments he has made. He's a pitcher to watch during spring training, as he'd have a top-25 starter's ceiling with a standout March.

name: Kyle Bradish
season_outlook: Bradish underwent Tommy John surgery with an internal brace in June 2024 but returned to start six games down the stretch. While command and control can lag after surgery, he showed little rust, striking out 47 batters against just 10 walks over 32 innings, with velocity in line with his healthy years. The performance was encouraging, but he has totaled only 104.2 innings across the majors and minors over the past two seasons. That likely points to workload management ahead, and expecting him to sustain last season's pace, even if it mirrors his healthy 2023, may be optimistic. A cautious approach is warranted.

name: Ryan Helsley
season_outlook: A plenty-productive fantasy closer for the Cardinals over the majority of the past two seasons -- his 610 points scored from the beginning of 2024 until his 2025 deadline trade were third-most among relief pitchers -- Helsley's numbers went right into the tank following his move into setup relief for the Mets. His prior control issues and difficulty minimizing hard contact came back to haunt him, as he had a 7.20 ERA in 22 games for his new team. Undeterred by this, the Orioles signed Helsley to a two-year deal to serve as their fill-in closer, a role from which his elite velocity and past experience should make him one of the better mid-round picks at the position.

name: Luis Castillo
season_outlook: Castillo has outpitched his peripherals since joining the Mariners in 2022, and it may be by design rather than just good fortune. With the Reds, Castillo was an extreme groundball pitcher which helped offset the homer-friendly Great American Ball Park. In the Pacific Northwest, he is leaning more on his four-seam fastball, which generates more flyballs. T-Mobile Park suppresses home runs, so while his home-run rate has risen, it remains reasonable, and the added flyballs are driving a BABIP between .267 and .285 over the past four seasons. The change in approach has sent his strikeout rate into freefall, denting his fantasy allure and increasing his dependence on a low BABIP, a slippery slope. Entering his age-33 season, Castillo's floor is more wobbly than usual, and without strikeouts, the ceiling is limited.

name: Tanner Bibee
season_outlook: Bibee fell ill with food poisoning and missed his Opening Day assignment, which set the tone for a queasy start to the 2025 season. He posted a 5.85 ERA through his first four outings for the Guardians, but the right-hander settled in and ultimately peaked at the right time with a 0.86 ERA and 0.71 WHIP over his final 21 regular-season innings to help Cleveland overtake Detroit for the AL Central crown. While Bibee does not possess an overpowering fastball, he has five secondary pitches, including a changeup that helps him neutralize lefty batters. His strikeout rate fell precipitously last season and lagged well behind the top-end arms in MLB. His home-run rate is also trending in the wrong direction, but Bibee limits walks and has pitched especially well at home at Progressive Field in his three seasons in the big-league rotation.

name: Robert Suarez
season_outlook: Suarez is coming off back-to-back top-10 fantasy closer seasons, his 76 saves during that time being MLB's most. However, let's address the elephant in the room following his departure from San Diego. He has an ERA nearly a full run higher away from Petco Park (3.41) than at it (2.44) for his career, with his other ratios reflecting a steep home/road split. Fortunately, Suarez's combination of high-90s average fastball velocity, elite control and balanced platoon splits should afford him a relatively soft landing in Atlanta's Truist Park -- a more hitter-friendly, but hardly heavenly, venue. Expect his ratios to rise, but as the Braves' clear closer, he should put forth another potential top-10 fantasy season at the position.

name: Emilio Pagan
season_outlook: For only the second time in his nine MLB seasons, Pagan seized hold of a closer opportunity and thrived in it, this time setting personal bests with his 56 games finished, 32 saves and 340 fantasy points (eight more than in his other closer year of 2019). A much-improved splitter had a lot to do with it, fueling career bests of a .161 BAA and .507 OPS allowed to lefties. That should ensure Pagan a long ninth-inning leash, though he's one of the greater risk/reward closers based upon his skill set, as an extreme fly baller whose control is only so-so. Draft Pagan in the middle rounds, once the higher-ceiling closers are gone.

name: Emmet Sheehan
season_outlook: Sheehan's return from May 2024 Tommy John surgery couldn't have gone much more smoothly, especially since he returned to big-league action in only 13 months. From July 6 forward, he scored 185 fantasy points, 17th among pitchers, while posting encouraging 30.6% strikeout and 7.6% walk rates that represented a definite step forward from his 2023 numbers. Sheehan was considered one of the better pitching prospects before the injury, so he should take another step forward, particularly in terms of volume, in 2026. The Dodgers might keep him on an innings cap, with 130-140 being a good guess, but that's plenty for him to warrant mid-round consideration in fantasy leagues.

name: Zac Gallen
season_outlook: After years of outperforming his expected ERA, Gallen didn't get much favor from Lady Luck in 2025. He had the eighth-widest ERA-xERA differential among qualifiers, he posted a career-worst 21.5% strikeout rate and he had an ERA over 4.00 in five out of six months. Still, Gallen continued to pitch effectively enough deep into games, his 33 starts being second-most and 192 innings eighth-most in the league. Plus, he had a 3.32 ERA over his final 11 starts. Back with the Diamondbacks after a long winter on the free-agent market, Gallen is a strong points-league option as one of the more durable starters out there.

name: Abner Uribe
season_outlook: Shaky control and a knee injury sustained during a game of Hacky Sack ruined Uribe's 2024, which began with the promise of potential save chances (including in four of the team's first six games). He'd settle for a middle relief role to begin 2025, from which he was every bit as excellent as he was across the final three months of his 2023 debut campaign. Uribe led the league in holds (37) and was third among relievers in both ERA and hard-hit rate allowed. Plus, he managed six saves and a 1.89 ERA in 18 games between the regular season and postseason after stepping back into the closer role for an injured Trevor Megill. That breakthrough puts Uribe in direct competition with Megill for the team's ninth-inning role this season, with your league's inclusion of saves or holds ultimately determining Uribe's value. He'll be one of the best closers or holds-getters, however it shakes out.

name: Jeff Hoffman
season_outlook: Reliever ERAs can be deceptive, and Hoffman was a clear example of that for several years. He beat his estimators in four straight seasons, running an ERA well below what his peripherals suggested. It led to expectations of regression, and his 4.37 ERA last year was his highest since 2021. Even so, a 3.21 SIERA suggests the results were inflated. While there was some skills slippage, potentially tied to a move into the AL East, the biggest problem was a sharp spike in home runs, as his 1.99 HR/9 ranked among the league's worst. Hoffman still recorded a career-high 33 saves, fourth most in baseball, but frequent long balls are a quick way to lose managerial trust, particularly in high-leverage spots like the postseason. He remains part of Toronto's saves picture, but opportunities will have to be earned, and limiting home runs will be critical.

name: Kenley Jansen
season_outlook: The active career leader in saves (476), Jansen's skills gradually eroded as he progressed through his mid-30s, but the Tigers see enough potential in him at age 38 that they signed him as their presumptive closer. He has saved at least 25 games in each of the past 13 uninterrupted MLB seasons, but 2025 saw him register career worsts in strikeout rate (24.4%), Statcast expected ERA (3.74) and hard-hit rate allowed (44.6%). Jansen is a role-driven, middle-of-your-staff type for fantasy purposes, the promise of save chances in Detroit buoying his value -- so long as he pitches effectively enough to keep the job.

name: Daniel Palencia
season_outlook: Coming off a 6.14 ERA and an unremarkable spring, Palencia opened the season at Triple-A Iowa before being recalled in mid-April to add bullpen depth. He quickly impressed, posting a 1.20 ERA and 0.80 WHIP with 15 strikeouts across 15 innings, which earned him a save opportunity amid struggles from Ryan Pressly and an injury to Porter Hodge. Though he blew his first chance, Palencia converted his next five save opportunities and retained the job until a shoulder injury sidelined him in early September. He returned for the final week in lower-leverage work. With the Cubs adding quality setup options, Palencia has a clear path to build on last year's team-leading 23 saves. While his track record is lacking, a repeat performance could elevate him into a higher tier.

name: Ryan Weathers
season_outlook: Weathers didn't make his season debut in 2025 until mid-May due to a forearm strain, and he landed back on the injured not long thereafter due to a lat injury. The left-hander finished the campaign with just eight starts, though he pitched well in those appearances with a 3.99 ERA, 1.28 WHIP and 37:12 K:BB over 38.1 innings. Weathers hasn't made more than 16 appearances in a season since working as a swingman as a rookie with the Padres in 2021. He has a 3.75 ERA and 1.21 WHIP across the past two seasons, but he simply hasn't been healthy enough to move the needle for fantasy managers. Weathers could factor into the Yankees' rotation for as long as he can take the mound, but he's likely to have a limited workload even if healthy given that he's yet to throw 100 frames in a season as a big leaguer.

name: Seth Lugo
season_outlook: After moving to a full-time starting role in 2023, Lugo survived with modest strikeout rates by limiting walks and suppressing home runs, helped by pitcher-friendly parks in Petco Park and Kauffman Stadium. He reached last season's break with a 2.67 ERA and 1.08 WHIP, seemingly following the same script, but a 4.17 xFIP hinted at looming issues. Elevated walk and home-run rates were hidden by an 87.9 percent left-on-base mark, and the correction came quickly. Over his final seven starts, Lugo posted an 8.35 ERA and 2.01 WHIP as his command and control unraveled, potentially tied to a back injury that ended his season early. On top of the strikeouts being a weak point, the late-season breakdown leaves added questions going forward.

name: Pete Fairbanks
season_outlook: Fairbanks remarkably avoided the injury bug in 2025 -- he had missed at least a month while on the IL in each of the previous four seasons -- and set personal bests with his 27 saves and 60 1/3 innings. While his raw stuff and underlying metrics, paled in comparison to his 2022-23 peak, he was plenty serviceable in the Rays' closer role. The Marlins, taking note of that and his 17 saves and 2.43 ERA away from homer-friendly George M. Steinbrenner Field, signed Fairbanks to handle their ninth inning, where he'll call a much more pitcher-friendly environment his home. Once the more durable, top-shelf relievers are off the board, this is a strong, risk/reward choice to fill out your pitching staff.

name: Ryan Pepiot
season_outlook: At casual glance, Pepiot's 2025 has the guise of �spinning his wheels� or worse, a small step backwards. His ERA rose by more than a quarter of a run, he averaged 0.1 fewer fantasy points per start, and he whiffed only 24.6% of the hitters he faced after 26.3% the year before. Make no mistake, however, that the Rays' return to Tropicana Field for 2026 is a huge positive for Pepiot, who surrendered 17 homers (among 26 total) at what was the majors' seventh most-favorable home run environment in 2025. He's a capable, now built-up starting pitcher who could be ready to take another step forward into top-25 SP territory.

name: Hunter Greene
season_outlook: First, the good: On a per-start basis, Greene's skills took a noticeable step forward in 2025, as he set personal bests with his 31.4% strikeout and 6.2% walk rates, 68.8% rate of first-pitch strikes and 99.5 mph average fastball velocity. Then, the bad: He spent more than a month on the IL for the fourth consecutive season, this time missing 85 days across two stints for a groin strain. It underscores Greene's risk/reward status for fantasy leagues, as his raw stuff makes him a legitimate Cy Young contender when he's healthy --which he unfortunately hasn't been fully across any of his four MLB seasons. Considering every pitcher seems to be an injury risk these days, however, and that Greene will play 2026 at a prime-age 26, reward seems to be the smarter driving draft-day force.

name: Trevor Megill
season_outlook: Handed the Brewers' closer role at the onset of last season following the trade of Devin Williams, Megill upped both his fastball velocity and strikeout rate to score the eighth-most fantasy points among relief pitchers through late August, when he was lost for a month due to a flexor strain. Megill would return in time for the Brewers' playoff run, although Abner Uribe's performance in the interim thrusts the position into somewhat of a spring competition entering 2026. Megill figures to be the favorite to close, with similar top-10 positional production after his back-to-back elite campaigns, though this is a situation to watch throughout March.

name: Bryan Abreu
season_outlook: Abreu joined the Triple-Digit Club for the third straight season, reaching 100 strikeouts yet again, with only Cade Smith and Mason Miller achieving the milestone twice over that span. Abreu spent most of the season setting up Josh Hader, recording 25 holds, but he was pressed into closing in mid-August and delivered seven saves in eight chances. Curiously, he posted a 4.24 ERA and 1.53 WHIP during that stretch, but it was fueled by an uncharacteristically high .442 BABIP, over 60 points higher than the mark he posted the previous two seasons. It is not clear if Hader will be ready to start the season, which will drive up Abreu's price. Abreu sits atop the list of closers-in-waiting with the ability to protect ratios while contributing to strikeouts.

name: Lucas Erceg
season_outlook: The Athletics traded Erceg to the Royals at the 2024 trade deadline, and after notching holds in his first five outings, he was installed as the closer. However, Kansas City signed Carlos Estevez in the offseason, relegating Erceg to setup duties last season. He delivered 23 holds and chipped in with a pair of saves and eight wins, but there was a noticeable change under the hood, as Erceg's strikeout rate plummeted nine points. His ERA was unaffected by the decline, as he posted a career-low mark, though estimators pegged it as more than a run too low. His velocity dropped a tick across the board, likely contributing to the strikeout dip. Erceg's season ended in mid-September with a shoulder impingement, but he's expected to be ready for camp. Monitor his velocity; without a rebound, he's risky as a reliable source of holds.

name: Griffin Jax
season_outlook: One of the unluckiest pitchers of 2025, with a league-high .362 BABIP, and the second widest ERA-FIP differential in the wrong direction, among qualified relievers, Jax could be one of the position's biggest sleepers with some correction in those departments. Combine his past two seasons and he has the third best K/BB ratio (5.49), fourth-best FIP (2.21), and 62 saves plus holds (18th among relievers), underscoring his elite skill set. As spring training dawns, the Rays don't have a clear closer, a role from which Jax could be a top-10 positional fantasy option if they shift off their longstanding tendency to �mix and match� out of the bullpen. He'll be a top source of holds or saves nevertheless, making him one of the top relievers to target once the clear, elite closers are off the board.

name: Jeffrey Springs
season_outlook: After returning from Tommy John surgery in 2024, Springs was traded from the Rays to the A's last offseason. He went on to pitch a career-high 171 innings in 2025, reaching the 30-start threshold for the first time at 32 years old. The left-hander struggled early on last season, particularly in the first inning, leading the team to experiment with an opener in front of Springs a couple times. His performance improved after some adjustments, though his numbers started to slip again around the middle of August. Nevertheless, in the end, Springs led the A's in ERA, wins and strikeouts among other categories, making him the de facto ace of the pitching staff entering 2026. The swing-and-miss is way down at this stage of his career, but Springs will get a chance to build upon what he showed over the final three months with regular starts for an improving team.

name: Carlos Estevez
season_outlook: Estevez is coming off a fantastic season for Kansas City which saw him lead all of baseball with 42 saves for an 82-win club. Any concerns the talented Lucas Erceg would steal saves were quickly set aside as Estevez refused to give up any ground in the bullpen. He does not have the big strikeout rates of other closers in the game, but over the past two seasons, Estevez has the third-lowest ERA of all active closers and does not get himself into trouble with walks or homers. The fact Kansas City plays in a high rate of late and close games due to an inconsistent offense only helps Estevez get the ball on a regular basis. Estevez is not the sexiest closer, but he gets the job done and he should one again save 30-plus contests in 2026.

name: Casey Mize
season_outlook: Mize hit the injured list in May with a hamstring strain but still made his first All-Star team in 2025, going 9-3 with a 3.15 ERA and 1.22 WHIP over 88.2 innings with Detroit in the first half. He slumped to a 4.92 ERA and 1.34 WHIP after the break, mirroring the team's collective slide. The right-hander shaved his walk rate to just 5.7 percent while upping his strikeout rate to a career-high 22.2 percent last season, though he got touched up with the long ball on occasion, with the splitter in particular yielding a surprising number of homers. After being drafted No. 1 overall in 2018, Mize underwent Tommy John surgery in 2022, missing the entire 2023 season as a result. No ace but from a bust, Mize has re-emerged in recent years as a capable mid-rotation arm for the Tigers.

name: Reid Detmers
season_outlook: Shifted to the bullpen full-time to begin 2025, Detmers added two ticks to his average fastball velocity and, after some early struggles, thrived in his new role. Over his final 49 appearances, he had a 2.19 ERA, three saves, 13 holds and a 33.5% strikeout rate. The Angels, perhaps seeing his improved stuff and control -- as well as considering his past history as a starter -- entered spring training planning to have him back in their rotation for 2026. With that move, Detmers' fantasy upside increases, but he’ll warrant careful examination to see whether he can first maintain his 2025 gains.

name: Seranthony Dominguez
season_outlook: Dominguez has settled in as a whiff-generating, righty-dominating, short reliever -- and one who has been popular on the midseason trade market -- making him a good pickup for the bullpen-starved White Sox. His experience could prove useful in a prospective spring closer competition with Grant Taylor and Jordan Leasure, though Dominguez would still be helpful in holds leagues if the team prefers to go with a younger option.

name: Bryce Miller
season_outlook: Coming off what was a top-10 fantasy starter's 2024, Miller's follow-up campaign was effectively ruined by bone spurs in his elbow, the ailment sending him to the IL twice and nearly doubling his ERA. Though his fastball velocity and whiff rate on his splitter improved over the season's final six weeks, his ERA over that time was nevertheless 5.62 and he couldn't find consistency at any point all year. Miller did avoid offseason surgery, but only spring training can demonstrate whether the winter's rest has helped him. He still has that ace-caliber stuff when healthy, so a strong spring would make him a potentially profitable late-round pick.

name: Roki Sasaki
season_outlook: Apparently, the fastball velocity drop he experienced in his final year in Japan was no mirage, as Sasaki struggled early in that regard in his first taste of the U.S. game, posting a 4.72 ERA and 15.6% strikeout and 14.3% walk rates in eight starts before a shoulder issue cost him the next three months. He'd return with elevated velocity and filthy stuff out of the bullpen in September and the playoffs, even handling some save chances in October, which offered a glimpse of his elite potential. Sasaki should be stretched out again to start this spring and, if he's looking similarly good -- monitor that velocity, which needs to be closer to 98 than 96 mph -- he'd be a breakout candidate, albeit one who might face an innings cap.

name: Jack Leiter
season_outlook: Leiter's adjustment to big-league competition has been slow, but appreciate his 2025 growth for what it was. He posted a 3.28 ERA, seven quality starts and a 26.3% strikeout rate across 13 second-half starts and lowered his walk rate to 7.0% over his final nine outings. Equipped with a high-90s fastball and maturing slider and changeup, Leiter could be ready to take a big step forward in 2026. He has the top prospect pedigree, making him one of the more potentially profitable prospective late-round picks for your draft.

name: Aaron Ashby
season_outlook: Ashby adapted brilliantly to a multi-inning reliever role in 2025, his blend of elite ground ball, strikeout and hard-hit rates giving him a strong base of raw skills. It's a profile that should make him one of the better relief wins/holds/matchups-driven saves combo types, though the Brewers do have a decision to make on him this spring: Does he remain in that role, or would he provide them more utility out of the rotation? Keep tabs on Ashby's spring usage, as he could be a matchups-oriented starter with some upside if stretched out for the role.

name: Jameson Taillon
season_outlook: Taillon averaged 30 starts per season over the prior four years but was limited to 23 last season after two second-half IL stints for a right calf strain and a left groin strain. Despite the missed time, he posted a sub-4.00 ERA for the third time in four seasons, even as his estimators have sat nearly a run higher the past two years. His strikeout rate has generally declined, though he showed a modest rebound compared to 2024, while his control remains near elite and his home-run rate tends to run high. In a retro draft, where players are selected based on that season's statistics, Taillon would have been a decent pick in three of the past four years. Looking ahead, the combination of modest strikeouts, home run vulnerability and emerging durability questions makes him a volatile option.

name: Ryan Walker
season_outlook: Unable to maintain the elevated strikeout rate that earned him the Giants' closer role over the final two months of 2024, Walker was demoted back to middle relief after posting a 6.43 ERA over his first 16 appearances last season. He'd ultimately get another chance to close in August and September following the trade of Camilo Doval, but Walker's slider wasn't nearly as effective in 2025 as in the past, and he ultimately finished the season with MLB's fourth-most blown saves (7). Walker should begin 2026 as the team's primary ninth-inning option, with good enough command and a ground-ball leaning that would make him a useful mid-range fantasy option, but he'd need to make a significant adjustment in order to vault into the position's top 10.

name: Jason Adam
season_outlook: A ruptured quadriceps tendon prematurely ended what was an otherwise excellent year for Adam in setup relief, as he turned in a second straight year of a sub-2.00 ERA and at least 25 holds and 70 strikeouts in 2025. Keep tabs on his health once spring training opens. When healthy, he’ll almost assuredly serve as Mason Miller’s primary setup man and fantasy insurance policy. Adam’s skill set is top-20 caliber among relief pitchers, so expect a return to that form sometime before midseason at the latest.

name: Jacob Latz
season_outlook: A handy swingman who was productive for the Rangers in both roles in 2025 (2.72 ERA in eight starts, 2.93 in 25 relief appearances), Latz figures to compete for a rotation spot this spring. It's the role from which he'd be more fantasy-relevant, even if only from a matchups perspective. His mediocre walk rate and penchant for fly balls puts him at heightened risk of bad outings, which would be a bigger deal if those outings are shorter. Should Latz emerge in the Rangers rotation, consider him in the late rounds as you're filling out your staff.

name: Tyler Rogers
season_outlook: A submarining, ground ball-generating, righty-dominating short reliever, Rogers is one of the very best at his craft. However, you need to recognize the craft -- that of a locked-in, primary setup man rather than a flamethrower -- for what it is. He's a holds machine, owning 18% of the total number of 30-hold seasons across the past five seasons (he has four), with some of the most projectable ratios around. That's a nice thing to have in formats that reward setup men.

name: Spencer Schwellenbach
season_outlook: Schwellenbach was well on his way towards earning Cy Young votes when a small fracture in his right elbow brought his 2025 to an abrupt stop in June. Between the final three months of 2024 and the first three of last season, he scored the fifth-most fantasy points among pitchers (502), thanks in part to a high-90s fastball and an elite, whiff-generating splitter. Unfortunately, Schwellenbach's elbow issues persisted through the winter, and he required Feb. 18 surgery to remove loose bodies from his elbow. The Braves placed him on the 60-day IL at the onset of spring training, so he'll miss at least the first two months of 2026 and perhaps more than that. Schwellenbach has the upside to be a top-20 option at his position when healthy, but he's as risky a pick as they come if you're aiming to stash him for the second half.

name: Joe Musgrove
season_outlook: Musgrove missed all of last season while rehabbing from the Tommy John surgery he underwent in October 2024, but he should be good to go for the start of 2026 given that he was throwing multi-inning bullpen sessions late last season. The veteran right-hander has a 3.25 ERA, 1.12 WHIP and 9.6 K/9 since the start of the 2020 campaign, but there are major question marks regarding his durability as he enters his age-33 season. Musgrove made just 36 starts across 2023 and 2024 due to injuries (even before the Tommy John injury), and he's now coming off a lost season and major elbow surgery. Regaining his strong form in the first year back wouldn't be unheard of, but Musgrove's additional injury issues add another layer to consider. His ceiling is that of a top-end starter, but the floor here is zero.

name: Luis Severino
season_outlook: Signed last winter to the largest guaranteed deal in Athletics franchise history, Severino threw six scoreless innings in Seattle on Opening Day before a harsh introduction to Sutter Health Park. The veteran right-hander struggled to a 6.01 ERA and 1.53 WHIP in 15 starts at home in 2025, compared to a 3.02 ERA and 1.07 WHIP on the road. He couldn't find a pitch to put hitters away and saw his strikeout rate fall to a career-low 17.6 percent. The results improved overall down the stretch, and Severino still throws hard for a starting pitcher, averaging 96.1 mph on his four-seamer last season. However, the skills are not what they once were. This will feel like playing with fire so long as he's pitching in Sacramento.

name: Yusei Kikuchi
season_outlook: Kikuchi found another gear after being traded to the Astros at the 2024 deadline, largely by shaving half a tick off his curve and changeup, which made his fastball play up. That showing led the Angels to sign him to a long-term deal, banking on some carryover. Instead, all of his pitches lost velocity last season, whether by design or age-related decline. The reduced velocity aided his offspeed and breaking pitches but hurt his four-seamer, contributing to his lowest strikeout rate since 2019 and his highest walk rate in three years. At 35 years old, and with 97 starts over the past three seasons, Kikuchi faces a number of questions including whether the velocity returns. The left-hander can still contribute, but his best use comes at home in favorable matchups.

name: Colin Rea
season_outlook: Rea transitioned from the Brewers to the Cubs in 2025 and posted a career-best 3.95 ERA with a 1.25 WHIP and 127:44 K:BB across 159.1 innings. He started in 27 of his 32 appearances and continues to provide value as a back-end starter, though his fantasy upside is limited given his 7.2 K/9 the past two seasons. Rea could work as more of a swingman for Chicago in 2026, though he should have a strong chance of opening the season in the rotation with Justin Steele expected to be unavailable for the first month or two of 2026 while rehabbing from elbow surgery.

name: Ryne Nelson
season_outlook: Nelson made some changes to his approach in 2025, and the results followed. He remains a fastball-heavy pitcher, but against lefties he used breaking balls rather than changeups as his secondary offerings and greatly improved his results. Lefties had hit .267/.328/.482 off him the previous two seasons, but the new approach led to a .191/.25/.309 outcome in 2025. Nelson also found more success pitching at home, which had been a tremendous problem for him each of the previous two seasons. Nelson did not even join the Arizona rotation on a full-time basis until early June but went 5-2 with a 3.38 ERA and 1.10 WHIP over those 20 starts. Nelson looks primed to repeat his 2025 success with more innings as a full-time starter who has worked hard to reduce some overall weak spots in his game.

name: Brady Singer
season_outlook: The sinkerballer almost made pitching in Cincinnati look easy in his first season with the Reds in 2025, posting a 3.29 ERA and 1.11 WHIP over 90.1 innings at Great American Ball Park. He was not as fortunate on the road, but Singer finished with 14 wins and 15 quality starts, providing much-needed stability at the back of the rotation for manager Terry Francona. It was a situation where the piece fit exactly as intended for the team, though there is little in the numbers to suggest another level could be lurking underneath the surface with Singer at 29 years old. While he generally keeps the ball in the park, the strikeout rate is modest. Many will want to avoid tough matchups at home even with his success last season, as the park can exacerbate the bad days.

name: Kodai Senga
season_outlook: Senga was as unhittable as any pitcher in baseball through the first third of the season. He won seven of his first 13 starts with a 1.47 ERA and 1.11 WHIP, striking out 24 percent of the batters he faced. An acute hamstring injury sent him to the injured list in mid-June, and that is when the fun ended. Senga came back for nine games after the injury, won none of them, and pitched to a 5.90 ERA and 1.69 WHIP while seeing his K-BB drop to an unsightly eight percent. Senga was eventually sent to Triple-A Syracuse and was not much better there. Senga's forkball is still amazing, but he had to use his non-forkballs too frequently to get back into counts. The Mets will hope an offseason of rest allows Senga to rediscover his early-2025 ways quickly in 2026.

name: Matthew Liberatore
season_outlook: Liberatore finally got a full-season look as a starter for the Cardinals, and he was a solid rotation piece with a 4.21 ERA, 1.31 WHIP and 122:40 K:BB across 151.2 innings. He fared better early in the season and had a 3.70 ERA at the end of June, but the career-high workload may have caught up with him a bit during the second half. He'll get plenty of runway to start in 2026 with the Cardinals finally going all-in on a rebuild, and he should be a bit more reliable in his second year as a full-time MLB starter, with a 6.2 percent walk rate giving him a strong base. However, Liberatore did give up a fair amount of hard contact and doesn't have much strikeout upside, so his ceiling is limited.

name: Chad Patrick
season_outlook: Patrick essentially came out of nowhere in 2025, delivering a 3.53 ERA, 1.28 WHIP and 127:40 K:BB across 119.2 innings for the Brewers as a rookie. He had some stints at Triple-A during the second half once Milwaukee's rotation got healthy, but he worked out of the bullpen during the closing stretch of the regular season and the playoffs. A 3-8 record was the only real blemish against him, as wins were difficult to come by at times with just six of his 23 starts lasting at least six innings. Patrick would have some fantasy upside if he can crack Milwaukee's starting unit in 2026, but he isn't guaranteed to be a regular member given the plethora of options the club has to round out the rotation.

name: Chris Bassitt
season_outlook: Bassitt keeps on keeping on as one of the game's more durable innings-eaters, totaling the 17th-most fantasy points among starting pitchers over the past four seasons, despite a No. 39 average annual finish in that department during that same time span. That's the benefit of locked-in, 30-start types in points leagues, especially those who possess Bassitt's combination of above-average control and ability to suppress fly balls and hard contact. He's an ideal guy to draft late and stream, especially against weaker teams, as he has an ERA nearly a run lower in his career against losing (3.19) than .500-plus (4.11) teams.

name: Dylan Lee
season_outlook: Lee put forth a second consecutive solid season in setup relief, his holds total swelling to a team-leading 19 in 2025. That he lowered his walk rate was a help, as that's one of the categorical fears among short relievers with the fly ball leaning he has (33.0 FB%). Lee should be one of the team's most trusted late-inning relievers again in 2026, though the addition of Robert Suarez, who should handle the eighth, might cap the lefty's holds ceiling around last year's total.

name: Will Vest
season_outlook: The Tigers opened the season without a defined closer, and Vest was not part of the early mix. After posting a 1.17 ERA and 0.52 WHIP with nine strikeouts in 7.2 innings, however, he earned the first of what became a team-leading 23 saves. Manager A.J. Hinch leaned most heavily on Vest while still playing matchups, which allowed him to add four holds. Illustrating reliever ERA volatility, Vest logged his highest ERA since 2022, even as his xFIP and SIERA were their lowest over that span. He is not as overpowering as the top-tier closers, but he fanned more than a batter per inning over the past three seasons. Detroit bolstered their bullpen with fellow right-handers Kenley Jansen and Kyle Finnegan, yet Hinch remains noncommittal on roles. Vest fits well in leagues that count holds, as he should continue to work in high-leverage spots regardless.

name: Grayson Rodriguez
season_outlook: Rodriguez did not make an appearance at any level in 2025. The right-hander first received a cortisone shot in March to treat elbow inflammation before suffering a lat strain in April. He was eyeing a return before the break but was shut down again in July with renewed elbow discomfort, a setback which eventually led to debridement surgery. The baseball world let out a collective groan when the Orioles subsequently shipped Rodriguez to the Angels in exchange for Taylor Ward, as many read it as an indictment of Rodriguez's arm health. GM Perry Minasian said after the move that he examined the medicals and gained confidence that Rodriguez will be over his problems in 2026. It's difficult to trust, but Rodriguez is a former top prospect who showed a high level in 2024 before the lost season.

name: Brayan Bello
season_outlook: Bello began the 2025 campaign on the injured list with a shoulder issue but returned to make 29 appearances (28 starts) for the Red Sox during the regular season before adding an abbreviated start in the wild-card round. While he put together his best season ever on the surface with a 3.35 ERA and 1.24 WHIP over 166.2 innings, the skills were largely similar to prior years, indicating good fortune over legitimate growth. Bello's game is predicated on keeping the ball on the ground with his sinker over the swing-and-miss, and that makes him subject to the whims of variance. Still just 26 years old to begin the 2026 season, Bello should be viewed as a detriment to WHIP, but he is at least a capable innings eater for Boston, having reached 28 starts and 157-plus innings each of the last three years.

name: Edwin Uceta
season_outlook: Control issues and an extreme fly ball-lean caused Uceta's 2025 to get off to a slow start, as he had a 5.53 ERA during the season's first half. Things improved from there, however, as he posted a 1.78 ERA and 35.5% strikeout rate in his 29 second-half appearances, re-establishing himself as one of the league's better setup relievers.
