With Pete Fairbanks no longer in Tampa Bay, Uceta could get a look in the ninth inning, whether full-time or as part of a committee arrangement. His skill set is likely to lead to game-over-game inconsistency, but the sum product should be that of a top-30 fantasy reliever.

name: David Peterson
season_outlook: Peterson is a 6-foot-6 lefty who gets good extension on his sinker, which allows him to keep the ball on the ground. He made a career-high 30 starts for the Mets in 2025, pitching to a 4.22 ERA and 1.37 WHIP over 168.2 innings. After throwing his first career shutout in June, Peterson was named to his first All-Star team, but his season went in the wrong direction from there. His final five starts were particularly ugly, with Peterson allowing 26 earned runs in 18.2 frames to skew the overall numbers. The groundball rate and advantageous home park can only do so much for a pitcher with marginal swing-and-miss, especially when the walk rate is a tad high. At 30 years old, he should continue to enjoy stretches of success when things are breaking right, but history says they will be fleeting.

name: Quinn Priester
season_outlook: Brought in to help patch up a Milwaukee rotation that was hit hard by injuries early on, Priester ended up playing a prominent role in the Brewers' 2025 success after struggling to find his footing between Pittsburgh and Boston to begin his career. The right-hander totaled 13 wins against three losses during the regular season for the best W-L percentage in all of baseball (.813). He was especially good during a 16-game stretch in the middle of the season in which he went 10-2 with a 2.74 ERA and 1.04 WHIP over 91 innings. A below-average strikeout rate should temper enthusiasm, but Priester keeps the ball on the ground and the Brewers have earned the benefit of the doubt when it comes to pitching. Perhaps an appeal to authority, this pick nonetheless makes sense in the later rounds.

name: Pablo Lopez
season_outlook: Lopez ended the 2025 season on the injured list with a forearm strain, and as Twins spring training dawned, it was revealed that he has a UCL tear in his right elbow and will require season-ending Tommy John surgery. Check back on his rehabilitation during 2027 spring training.

name: Kyle Leahy
season_outlook: Thanks in large part to greater reliance upon, and performance from, his curveball, Leahy cut 128 points off his OPS split against lefties in what was ultimately a breakthrough 2025. The Cardinals, seeing this, are giving him a long look as a starter this spring, with the adjustment elevating his fantasy potential (particularly on the matchups front). Leahy's upside might not be great, but if he's throwing well and emerges in the rotation in March, he'd warrant deep-mixed or NL-only consideration.

name: Jose Berrios
season_outlook: Berrios has logged the third-most innings since over the past five seasons, trailing only Logan Webb and Kevin Gausman, and it may have finally caught up with him. Berrios' season ended with right elbow inflammation which kept him off the postseason roster and potentially out of the 2026 Jays rotation. The club signed both Dylan Cease and Cody Ponce in the offseason, and it has said the latter was added as a starter. That currently leaves Berrios on the outside looking in unless Trey Yesavage falls into the same missteps Bowden Francis did this past season. Berrios' skills have slowly been eroding but it would be surprising to see him left out of the rotation all season as the club defends its AL pennant. The uncertainty around the status of his right arm may keep Berrios just cheap enough on draft day to turn him into an endgame value for 2026.

name: Bryan King
season_outlook: King made huge strides with both his control and command of what would otherwise be a lackluster fastball-sweeper combo last season, posting a 2.78 ERA and MLB’s ninth-most holds (27). Though he struggled to keep the ball in the yard (10 HR), he’s generally good enough at minimizing hard contact that he should improve in that department in 2026. Consider him a top source of holds, with fantasy-worthy ratios.

name: Max Scherzer
season_outlook: The Blue Jays keep stocking rotational depth, re-signing the future hall-of-famer at the end of February for a fraction of what he signed for last year. While Scherzer is coming off one of his worst seasons and is an injury risk who has fallen short of 20 starts in back-to-back years, he still has enough moxie to help fantasy managers on a matchups basis. AL-only managers can regard him a late rounder, but in standard formats, seek those games against weaker lineups or in road pitching friendly parks.

name: Cody Ponce
season_outlook: After a pair of so-so seasons for the Pirates (2020-21), followed by three nondescript seasons in Japan (2022-24), Ponce moved to the Korea Baseball Organization for 2025 and immediately flourished. Thanks to his adding a couple notches of velocity to his fastball while introducing a kick-change, he set the KBO single-season record for strikeouts (252) and won the league's Choi Dong-won Award (their Cy Young equivalent). Ponce returns to MLB with the Blue Jays, whose focus on optimizing pitchers' repertoires was exhibited on the national stage last October, meaning he's a good fit to his new surroundings. Pitchers returning from overseas don't often approach their statistical levels there -- scouts liken KBO competition to our Double-A ball -- but he could at least serve as a volume-oriented matchups play or back-of-a-staff mixed-league pick.

name: Shane Smith
season_outlook: It's becoming more common for players selected during the Rule 5 Draft to stick around with their new club, but it's not often that they end up being one of their new team's best players. That was the case for Smith, whom the White Sox selected from the Brewers during the 2024 Rule 5 Draft. The right-hander posted a 3.81 ERA, 1.20 WHIP and 145:58 K:BB across 146.1 innings during 2025, leading the Chicago rotation in most major categories. He limited the long ball pretty well with a 1.0 HR/9 but gave up a lot of hard contact, so there is some risk of regression, especially given the underwhelming defense behind him. Still, Smith has upside and could take a step forward in year two, and he should have plenty of volume on the rebuilding White Sox in 2026.

name: Dean Kremer
season_outlook: Kremer surpassed 170 innings for the second time in three seasons. His ERA was its highest during that span, though his estimators were the lowest. Kremer's modest strikeout rate leads to more variance than more dominant arms, but he shows solid control and command to help keep his ratios around league average. In 2022 and 2024, he failed to reach 130 innings, so he cannot be counted on for a full season. The AL East is not an ideal division for streamers, but the Orioles have fortified their offense with Pete Alonso and strengthened their bullpen with Ryan Helsley, making Kremer an option for favorable matchups in deeper formats.

name: Brandon Pfaadt
season_outlook: Pfaadt didn't pitch as poorly as his 5.25 ERA indicates, but getting back on track will require more than regression. His 4.01 xFIP and 4.12 SIERA paint a more encouraging picture, as a low 66.5 percent left-on-base rate inflated his ERA. At the same time, a sizable drop in his swinging-strike rate drove a sharp decline in strikeouts, and a modest reduction in his walk rate wasn't enough to counter it. Pfaadt adjusted his pitch mix by throwing fewer four-seam fastballs and sliders while adding a cutter and leaning more on his changeup and curve. Because his four-seamer and slider generate most of his swing-and-miss, the shift coincided with a loss of dominance. His 18.8 strikeout-minus-walk percentage from the prior season supported optimism, but the 14.3 percent mark in 2025 is concerning heading into 2026.

name: Hurston Waldrep
season_outlook: After receiving his first taste of the majors in 2024 with two starts, Waldrep spent the 2025 campaign with Triple-A Gwinnett before making his season debut for Atlanta in early August. The right-hander was one of the best starting pitchers in baseball down the stretch, going 6-1 with a 2.88 ERA, 1.19 WHIP and 55:22 K:BB in 56.1 innings across 10 appearances, and he gave up more than three runs in just one of those outings. Unfortunately, the 2023 first-round pick underwent surgery in February to remove loose bodies from his right elbow, likely shelving him for at least the first two months of the season. Waldrep has a high ceiling and could be Atlanta's next home-grown, standout starter, once he's healthy enough to return.

name: Lucas Giolito
season_outlook: Giolito’s 2025 return from an internal brace surgery looked like a win for his on-field and fantasy teams, as he posted his lowest ERA in six years, but even a cursory glance under the hood reveals troubling trends. His strikeout rate (19.7%) dipped to its lowest number in seven years, his Statcast expected ERA was 5.06, and he finished the year on the shelf, missing the Red Sox’s Wild Card Series due to an elbow injury. Giolito lingered on the free-agent market deep into the winter, raising further concerns as he enters his age-31 season. If he lands in a good spot and opens spring training as a favorite for a rotation spot, he can be a matchups play or volume-oriented points-league late rounder. However, his prior lofty ceiling is in his past.

name: Kirby Yates
season_outlook: For about one month of 2025, Yates looked like the top-shelf fantasy reliever he was in 2024, albeit exchanging saves for holds in L.A., but a hamstring injury in May threw derailed him and never afforded him the opportunity to get his season back on track. Despite this, the Angels signed him to compete, and perhaps serve as the favorite, for their closer role. So, who is the real Yates? The answer is probably something in-between his past two seasons, though it'll bring a lot of injury risk now that he's 39 years old. He's as risk/reward as prospective closers come.

name: Sean Manaea
season_outlook: The veteran southpaw logged a career-high 181.2 innings with the Mets in 2024 before crashing back to earth in 2025, as injuries sabotaged both workload and performance. While rehabbing an oblique strain, Manaea required a cortisone shot to combat a loose body in his left elbow, which delayed his season debut until July 13. From there, he largely struggled, allowing nearly two homers per nine. The strikeout and walk numbers were impressive, indicating the potential for a bounce-back season in the New York rotation, if healthy. The loose body has not been surgically removed but Manaea nonetheless said in November that he considers it a thing of the past, adding that he hopes to pitch the rest of his career without needing an operation on it.

name: Zack Littell
season_outlook: Littell’s pinpoint control makes up for his otherwise lackluster stuff, as over the last two seasons combined, he has an ERA (3.73) more than a third of a run lower than league average, despite a strikeout rate (19.2%) that’s more than 3% worse than average. He should again serve as a reliable MLB fourth starter, racking up useful innings for points-based fantasy teams, though he’s a difficult pitcher to stream because of his relatively balanced splits against good and bad opponents. If he lands in the right place, Littell can effectively round out your fantasy staff in deeper leagues.

name: Gabe Speier
season_outlook: Thanks to improved fastball velocity and the return of his whiff-generating slider, Speier emerged as a late-inning force for the AL West champion Mariners in 2025. His 24 holds ranked 16th in the league, and sixth among lefties. Plus, he lowered his walk rate to a sparkling 4.5%, fifth-best among qualified relievers. Speier returns as one of the team's primary setup men, from which he should again fill fantasy teams' holds and K's categories.

name: Jose Alvarado
season_outlook: An 80-game suspension for PEDs cut out a chunk of Alvarado's 2025, but on either side of it, he exhibited top-shelf velocity and improved control, which led to him totaling seven saves and five holds in 28 total appearances. While the Phillies' midseason acquisition of Jhoan Duran probably locks Alvarado into their primary lefty specialist role, it's still one from which he can rack up many holds and strikeouts.

name: Tyler Holton
season_outlook: After absorbing a massive workload (100 IP combined between the regular season and postseason) during the Tigers' 2024 Cinderella playoff run, Holton's fantasy numbers (as well as his underlying metrics) took a small, predictable step backwards last year. Righties hit him harder, he surrendered more hard contact overall, and he surrendered a whopping 15 homers. Holton did manage 17 holds nevertheless, and he'll remain a key piece in A.J. Hinch's matchups-oriented bullpen. There should be enough opportunity here to keep Holton as a solid source of holds and K's for fantasy purposes.

name: Justin Sterner
season_outlook: With Mason Miller now in San Diego, opportunities abound at the back of the Athletics bullpen. Sterner, who thrived late with a 1.40 ERA, 34.0% strikeout rate and seven holds over the final two months of 2025, should capture a late-round role, from which he'll add many holds and/or saves to the mix. An extreme fly ball lean (34.1% rate), coupled with the team's hitter-friendly home environment in Sutter Health Park, does put him at some risk for blow-ups, but he's a potential sleeper among late-round relievers.

name: Zebby Matthews
season_outlook: On the surface, Matthews' second taste of the majors didn't go that much better than the first. But upon closer examination, there was a lot to like about his 16-start performance, which sets him up to be a full-time starter for the rebuilding Twins. Matthews' ERA-FIP differential was the third widest (in the wrong direction) among pitchers with at least as many as his 79 1/3 innings, and he earned above-average grades for his velocity, control and ability to suppress hard contact. He's a sleeper among pitchers available in the latter rounds of mixed-league drafts, especially if he's throwing well during spring training.

name: Shawn Armstrong
season_outlook: In his 11th MLB season and with team No. 8, Armstrong set personal bests in games (71), innings (74), WHIP (0.81), BAA (.157), saves (9) and holds (12), thanks mostly to much better performance with his secondary pitches. He returned to his first big-league organization (Cleveland) during the offseason, where he'll serve as a setup man in the Guardians' well-stocked bullpen. Armstrong should be a reliable source of holds and ERA for fantasy teams in that role.

name: Simeon Woods Richardson
season_outlook: Woods Richardson again served as a back-end starter for Minnesota in 2025, though at one point it looked as though he could be exiting the rotation after posting a 5.74 ERA in his first nine outings. The right-hander closed out the campaign with a 3.00 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 68:29 K:BB in 69 frames across his final 14 appearances, posting a 5-1 record during that stretch. He improved his strikeout production to 8.6 K/9 but also gave out more free passes (3.7 BB/9). Woods Richardson has a higher floor but a lower ceiling than teammate Taj Bradley, and the two could be in competition for a spot in Minnesota's starting rotation during spring training.

name: Cole Sands
season_outlook: A 2024 breakthrough reliever for the Twins, Sands' numbers took a step backwards last season, in large part because he was largely unlucky on batted balls. His ERA was nearly three-quarters of a run higher than Statcast's expected, though he also warrants some blame for having middling whiff and hard-hit rates, pointing to what were good-not-great underlying skills. As one of the team's more experienced relievers, however, Sands should be part of a spring closer competition, and we'll see whether saves or holds are his categorical target come Opening Day.

name: Calvin Faucher
season_outlook: Faucher, who inherited the Marlins' closer job over the final two months of 2024, served as the leader of a committee last season, putting forth effective-yet-unspectacular stats. He finished with 15 saves and a second straight year of a sub-3.30 ERA, though his 4.25 FIP suggests he's due for some regression. That the Marlins signed Pete Fairbanks to close probably pushes Faucher back into a primary setup role, from which he'd be more of a middling holds source. Consider him a matchups-driven reliever with a shot at some saves should Fairbanks' past injury issues resurface.

name: Cade Povich
season_outlook: Povich's second major-league season in 2025 looked much like his rookie campaign, with a 5.21 ERA and 1.50 WHIP being quite similar, just with a larger workload. The left-hander improved both his strikeout and walk numbers (to 9.5 K/9 and 3.4 BB/9), but he surrendered too much hard contact for those improvements to matter. The Orioles have made some big splashes this offseason by signing Pete Alonso and trading for Shane Baz, and Zach Eflin is also back in the rotation mix. Since Baltimore is looking to immediately get back into playoff contention, Povich likely won't have much runway to iron out any troubles if he continues to struggle in the big leagues. The left-hander will likely need a strong showing during spring training to have a chance of cracking the Opening Day rotation, and even then there's no guarantee he sticks around for long.

name: Reese Olson
season_outlook: Olson opened the season strong, delivering a 2.96 ERA and 1.17 WHIP with 51 strikeouts across 48.2 innings in nine starts. A bout of right ring finger inflammation sidelined him for nearly seven weeks, and after returning he lasted only four more starts before a right shoulder strain ended his year. Those final outings were less sharp, as he recorded a 3.60 ERA and 1.30 WHIP with 14 strikeouts in 20 innings. Olson has shown effectiveness when available, but durability remains an issue, as he's yet to exceed 22 starts or 113 innings. He's expected to open the year in the Tigers' rotation, and his per-start output plays well, particularly in formats with dedicated IL spots.

name: Yimi Garcia
season_outlook: A barrage of injuries (shoulder, ankle, elbow) sidelined Garcia for much of 2025 and cost him the Blue Jays' run into the World Series. However, following surgery for the latter, he's expected to be ready to rejoin their bullpen come Opening Day. He still possesses that five-pitch repertoire of whiff-generating goodness and, if he's throwing well in March and claims a seventh- or eighth-inning role, he could be a discount source of holds and K's. Bear in mind, however, that Garcia's injury history makes him one of the position's riskier picks.

name: JP Sears
season_outlook: Sears opened the 2025 campaign as a rotation regular for the A's but finished it as a spot starter for the Padres, who acquired him in the Mason Miller deal at the trade deadline. Sears has never offered a ton of fantasy upside, but he regressed across the board last season with a 5.04 ERA, 1.32 WHIP and 117:36 K:BB in 27 starts. He's served up at least 28 home runs each of the past three seasons and doesn't offer much strikeout potential. Sears profiles as a back-end innings eater more than anything else, but as a contending club the Padres aren't likely to give him such an extended leash if the troubles persist, which was evident in 2025 as he made just five big-league starts after being traded to San Diego.
